chunks: "The first thing most people reach for is infrared.
An IR thermometer or a small thermopile sensor looks at the surface and infers temperature from the radiation it emits, and a thermal camera does the same for a whole image.
That's handy for a moving shaft or a commutator because nothing touches it. The big catch is emissivity: painted or black surfaces emit well, around 0.
95, but bare shiny metal might be 0. 1, so an IR gun set for 0. 95 aimed at a bright shaft at 100 degrees might read 35.
I'd put a bit of matte tape or black paint on the spot, or calibrate against a contact reading.
Other options: you can infer temperature electrically without touching anything, from the winding's resistance, or from drift in the back-EMF constant for the magnets.
A thermal model fed by current and speed can estimate winding and rotor temperatures. For a rotor in a lab, I'd use wireless telemetry or a slip ring with an embedded sensor.
Fibre-optic sensors work in high-voltage and high-EMI places. And for a cheap check, temperature-indicating paint or labels change colour irreversibly at a set temperature.
Practical issues are spot size, so the sensor sees only the part I care about; reflections from hot surroundings; and windows, because ordinary glass blocks long-wave IR."
